Nigerian Startups Reclaim Top Spot in Africa With $635M
web.description:
# Nigerian Startups Reclaim Top Spot in Africa as Funding Hits $635 Million in 2026
![Omorogie Alele](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/8d049b3679fac95bea9a0f07c444d6414c6232c70324d5860615e35149a06143?s=96&d=mm&r=g)

By [Omorogie Alele](https://ventureburn.com/author/adele/)

22 October 2026

[![google-news](https://ventureburn.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/google-news-icon.png)](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqKggKIiRDQklTRlFnTWFoRUtEM1psYm5SMWNtVmlkWEp1TG1OdmJTZ0FQAQ?ceid=US:en&oc=3)

Key Takeaways

- Nigeria secured $635M in startup funding so far in 2026 to reclaim the number one position.
- The total funding was led by 4 massive scale-ups contributing 69% of the total startup funding.

![Nigerian startups have shattered recent records, raising an astonishing $635 million in just nine months.](https://ventureburn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/internal_upload_39CrNUO3SFuV374EJv_pPQ.jpg)

But the narrative has forcefully shifted. By the close of the third quarter, Nigerian startups reclaim top spot in Africa, pulling in a staggering $635 million.

That is not just a marginal victory. It highlights a return of VC capital into the country, as its funding through the first three quarters more than doubles the $247 million raised during the same window last year.

## The Heavyweights Driving the Mega-Rounds
Africa: The Big Deal [reported](https://thebigdeal.substack.com/p/q32026c) that Nigerian startups pulled in $635 million through the first three months, taking the top spot.

Investors are definitely writing massive checks, but they are aiming them exclusively at proven scale-ups with serious traction. Four specific companies accounted for 69% of the national total: up $440 million.

You really have to look at the underlying message here.

## The Great Sector Shift: Logistics Dethrones Fintech
Why? Because this isn’t a random blip on a spreadsheet.

![](https://ventureburn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Funding-raised-by-startups-in-Africa.jpg)

Funding raised by startups in Africa Q1-Q3

For the better part of seven long years, fintech was the undisputed king of African venture capital. Not anymore.

Across the continent, these mobility startups raised a towering $780 million in just nine months. They captured 36% of all venture funding, forcing fintech into the passenger seat at 35%.

This pivot fundamentally changes the startup playbook.

## Leaving the Rest of the Continent Behind

web.description:
African startups raised **$1.44 billion in the first half of 2026** — slightly ahead of the $1.42 billion raised in H1 2025, but across far fewer deals: just 146 disclosed rounds versus 252 a year earlier.

## All 30 at a glance
| Startup | Country | Sector | Round | 2026 amount |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| Taurex | Nigeria / Global | Fintech / trading | Series C | $40M |
| Stabyl | Nigeria | Fintech | Pre-seed | $2.7M |

## The growth rounds: debt does the heavy lifting
**Zeno**, the battery-swap motorcycle maker operating in East Africa, raised **$25 million** in March.

## The Series A club — and Morocco's quiet breakout
**WafR** raised a **$4 million seed** in January for retail-tech, and **Enakl** took **$2.3 million** to modernise shared commuting in Casablanca.

Under $3M • Seed & pre-seed

## The early-stage survivors: small cheques, sharp theses
In AI, Nairobi's **AethexAI** raised a **$3 million pre-seed** led by 4DX Ventures and Enza Capital to build customer-support and voice automation for African markets ( [our full breakdown](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/aethexai-raises-3-million-2026)). In fintech, Nigeria's **Stabyl** closed **$2.7 million** led by KongaPay in late June; **Daya** raised **$2.4 million** from Hivemind Capital for stablecoin-powered enterprise payments ( [deal notes](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/daya-raises-2-4-million-2026)); South Africa's **NjiaPay** banked a **$2.1 million seed** led by Newion for payment orchestration; and **Sika Financial** took **$2 million** from Aruwa Capital for cross-border settlement rails between Ghana and Nigeria ( [inside the deal](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/sika-financial-raises-2-million-2026)).

**Zimi Charge** raised **$2.6 million** from the Development Bank of Southern Africa and Keyo Ventures for EV charging in South Africa. **Breaze Delivery** raised **R20 million (~$1.23 million)** from Knife Capital and Kalon Venture Partners for township e-commerce logistics ( [our coverage](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/breaze-delivery-raises-2026)), and **Eja-Ice** secured **$1 million** from All On for off-grid solar cold-chain in Nigeria ( [deal notes](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/eja-ice-raises-1-million-2026)).

web.title: How Seed Funding For African Startups Creates Jobs and Wealth
web.description:
Every year, thousands of African founders build something worth funding.

In 2025, African startups raised somewhere between $3.8 billion and $4.1 billion in total, depending on which tracker you trust. Debt financing alone hit a record $1.64 billion, up 63% year on year.

Of the startups that raised seed funding in 2022, only about 10 in 100 had closed a Series A within 34 months, based on Condia’s State of Startup Funding in Africa report.

## Seed Funding For African Startups: The Current State (2025-2026 Data)
Equity financing, the traditional form of venture capital where investors take a stake in the company, grew more modestly, rising 8% year on year to $2.4 billion across 462 deals.

The picture gets more serious at pre-seed.

AVCA’s mid-year report found that seed-stage funding actually climbed 40% to $171 million across 82 early-stage transactions in the first half of 2025 alone.

Of the cohort that raised seed funding in 2021, only 5.1% successfully raised a Series A within two years.

## Why African Startups Struggle to Raise Seed Capital
Several historic pre-seed investors have either withdrawn from the market or repositioned their funds toward later, safer stages.

## Where to Find Seed Funding For African Startups
**Venture capital firms** remain the largest source of formal seed and early-stage funding. Ingressive Capital offers seed funding of up to $500,000 in exchange for around 10% equity in tech-enabled startups, alongside strategic guidance and networking support. Ajim Capital provides financing from pre-seed to seed with typical check sizes up to $250,000.

## How Much Seed Funding Can African Startups Raise?
But there are useful benchmarks.

Most African seed rounds fall between $500,000 and $2 million, with pre-money valuations typically between $3 million and $8 million. Fintech startups and those based in Nigeria, Kenya, or Egypt tend to raise toward the higher end of that range, since these markets have deeper investor pools and more comparable deals to benchmark against. Startups in less-covered markets, or in sectors that investors understand less well, often raise less, even with similar traction.

Grants tend to be much smaller and more standardized. The Tony Elumelu Foundation, for example, offers a flat $5,000 non-refundable grant.

Asking for a $10 million valuation with minimal traction, because a competitor raised at that level, tends to backfire. If you raise at an inflated valuation and don’t grow into it, your next round becomes much harder to close.

## The Future of Seed Funding for African Startups
Angel investing is likely to become even more central to the earliest stages of funding, filling the gap left by the withdrawal of some historic pre-seed players.

## Conclusion
Seed funding for African startups is not scarce in the way it’s sometimes described.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Seed Funding For African Startups
### How much seed funding can an African startup raise?
Fintech startups and those based in Nigeria, Kenya, or Egypt tend to raise toward the higher end; startups in less-covered markets often raise less.

web.title: IFC Startup Catalyst
web.description:
# IFC Startup Catalyst
Investing in Accelerators and Early-Stage Funds

The Platform allows IFC to make relatively small investments, usually $4-6 million, in accelerators and seed funds focused on markets with nascent VC ecosystems, often as their first institutional investor. In addition to investment capital, IFC Startup Catalyst provides funds and accelerators with access to networks, training, and sector expertise.

## Results (as of FY26)
- $111 millionInvested in Funds
- 30accelerators and early-stage funds

## Startup Catalyst by Region
### Africa
IFC invested in Catalyst Fund Resilience I, L.P. (“Catalyst Fund”) in 2026. [Catalyst Fund](https://www.thecatalystfund.com/) is a pan-African pre-seed fund that invests in startups building climate adaptation and resilience solutions across Africa.

IFC invested in LoftyInc Alpha Fund, LLC (“LoftyInc Capital”) in 2025. [LoftyInc Capital](https://loftyinc.vc/) is a pan-African venture capital fund with offices in Nigeria, Egypt, and Kenya that invests in seed and Series A technology startups.

IFC invested in Pamoja Ventures, LP (“P1 Ventures”) in 2024.  [P1 Ventures](https://www.p1.ventures/) is a Nigeria-based early-stage venture capital fund with a pan-Africa mandate, that invests in artificial intelligence, machine learning, e-commerce, fintech, healthtech, insurtech, and SaaS sectors.

IFC invested in Ventures Platform Fund IV (“Ventures Platform”) in 2022.  [Ventures Platform](https://www.venturesplatform.com/) is a Lagos-based seed fund that invests in tech and tech-enabled startups across Africa, with emphasis on Nigeria.

IFC invested in Ventures Platform Pan-African Fund II (“Ventures Platform Fund II”) in 2025. [Ventures Platform](https://www.venturesplatform.com/) Fund II is a Lagos-based seed fund that invests in technology startups across Africa and builds on IFC’s 2022 investment in the manager’s previous fund.

### Europe
IFC invested in Flyer One Ventures Fund V C.V.

### Global

Nigeria startup funding reached US$635 million in the first nine months of 2026, reclaiming Africa’s top position for the first time since 2022.

Nigerian startups raised US$635 million between January and September 2026. That compares with US$247 million in the same period of 2025 — a 157 per cent increase, according to funding data published in October 2026. The result returned Nigeria to the continent’s startup-funding lead.

By FurtherAfrica’s reading of the numbers, the rebound reflects a small group of large transactions.

## **Large rounds drive the rebound**
[Moove](https://www.moove.io/) led the charge. The mobility fintech raised US$250 million in a Series C in August 2026, reaching a reported valuation of US$2.1 billion.

Source: October 2026 funding reports

Moove’s round alone represented approximately 68 per cent of Nigeria’s August 2026 funding. That single month generated around US$364 million — illustrating how quickly one large deal can reshape a country’s annual ranking.
